The energy that goes out always equals the energy that comes in. That is the first law of thermodynamics, and this bench checks it at every step.
Here you can build your machine, test it with real physics and see where every joule of energy goes, before spending anything on building it.

Villard de Honnecourt drew it around 1235.

Seven mallets hang from hinges on the rim of the wheel. On the descending side they swing outwards; on the rising side they hang close in. The idea is that the open side weighs more and the wheel never stops.

The open mallets are further from the axle, but there are always more mallets on the rising side. The two effects cancel out and the wheel settles into a position of balance. On top of that, every time a mallet falls against its stop it loses energy in the impact: see the “Impacts” line in the ledger.
A variant with rolling balls, repeated by inventors since the 17th century.
Eight slanted compartments with a steel ball in each. On one side the balls roll towards the rim and on the other towards the centre.

Same as with the mallets: there are fewer far-out balls than close-in ones, and the wheel stays balanced. Every time a ball rolls and hits the wall of its compartment it loses energy. Give it a push with your finger during the test and see how long it lasts.
Described by Bishop John Wilkins in the 17th century.
A magnet at the top pulls a steel ball up a ramp. Before it gets there, the ball drops through a hole and rolls back down another ramp to start again.

A magnet's force falls off very quickly with distance. From the bottom it barely pulls, and the ball rolls downhill. During the test, drag the ball towards the magnet with your finger: if you let go far away, it rolls back; if you let go a few centimetres away, the magnet catches it and never lets go. A magnet strong enough to pull it up from the bottom wouldn't let it fall through the hole either.
An idea repeated in countless internet videos.
A wheel with eight slanted magnets turns past three fixed magnets. The idea is that the magnets always push in the same direction.

The force between magnets, like gravity, gives back what it takes: what pushes on the way in brakes on the way out. In the ledger you'll see that all the energy it spends comes from the initial spin: over a full turn, the magnets give and take nothing. The wheel slows down from friction and finally gets stuck at a “sticky point”.
A test to check the bench itself.
A pendulum hanging from a ball bearing. It shows how much the air and the axle slow things down.

In the “Test” tab, turn on “Ideal world”: it will swing without stopping and its energy will stay the same. Then tap the hinge and connect the generator: the energy it takes out is exactly what the pendulum loses, and it stops. Without friction something can move forever, but it can't produce energy.
A motor and a generator on the same axle is one of the most repeated ideas.
A heavy flywheel with a generator and a motor on the same axle. The generator produces electricity and the motor uses it to keep pushing the wheel.

No generator or motor is perfect: the generator turns 85 % of what it brakes into electricity, and the motor turns 80 % of that electricity into push. Almost a third is lost as heat on every trip around the loop. Look at the “Heat” line in the ledger: that's why the flywheel slows down.
Six magnets on the rim of the wheel and a fixed electromagnet that switches on just as a magnet approaches, to pull it in, and switches off as it passes.

This wheel really does keep turning, but only because the battery gives it energy every time the electromagnet switches on. In the ledger you'll see the battery puts in far more than the wheel gains: almost all of it goes into heating the coil. Remove the battery (erase the electromagnet) and it stops.
